study: Does decoupling instruction fetch fix the pipeline's loss under memory latency?
answer: Yes, and it inverts the result. The pipeline now wins at every non-zero latency, and the margin grows with latency.
benchmark: hello.c, 297 instructions, every configuration verified against Spike
note: LATENCY counts wait states. The single-cycle core uses a blocking instruction port; the pipelined core uses a pipelined one plus a 4-entry prefetch buffer. That is not an unfair advantage - it is the architectural difference. A single-cycle core cannot exploit a pipelined port because it has nowhere to put an instruction it is not ready to execute.
cost_at_zero_latency: 484 cycles against 422 before. The prefetch buffer registers its response, so an instruction takes one extra cycle to reach decode. With ideal memory that is pure overhead - which is exactly why the earlier magic_mem-only comparison could never have shown the pipeline in a good light.
why_it_works: Fetch latency now overlaps with work already in flight instead of stopping the core. The margin GROWS with latency (1.17x, 1.51x, 1.84x), which is the signature of genuine overlap rather than a constant offset.
what_this_corrects: Two earlier claims of mine. First, that the pipeline only looked slower because magic_mem hid the cost of memory - the latency sweep disproved that, since the penalty flattened at 29%. Second, the diagnosis that followed: that the missing piece was a fetch buffer. That one held, but only together with a pipelined memory port. Neither alone changes anything, because a buffer cannot fill from a memory that serves one request at a time.
